claim: The epidermis is fueled by a basal layer of stem cells which are actively proliferating and continually differentiating apically to build the outer layers of the skin barrier.
source: The epidermis is fueled by a basal layer of stem cells which are actively proliferating and continually differentiating apically to build the outer layers of the skin barrier. (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a well-established description of epidermal biology supported by the figure reference and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing data has shown that the cell identity transition through epidermal differentiation is progressive and takes place over several days.
source: Recently, single-cell RNA-sequencing data has shown that the cell identity transition through epidermal differentiation is progressive and takes place over several days. Specifically, cells within the basal stem cell layer show global transcriptional changes associated with differentiation preceding exit from the basal layer (Aragona et al., 2020; Cockburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Aragona et al., 2020; Cockburn et al., 2022).

claim: Cells within the basal stem cell layer show global transcriptional changes associated with differentiation preceding exit from the basal layer.
source: Specifically, cells within the basal stem cell layer show global transcriptional changes associated with differentiation preceding exit from the basal layer (Aragona et al., 2020; Cockburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: High H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity correlates with heterochromatin (H3K9me3).
source: Fixed epidermal tissue expressing H2B-GFP (green) and co-stained with Hoechst or various subnuclear compartment markers (magenta), demonstrating that high H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity correlates with heterochromatin (H3K9me3), lower H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity correlates with euchromatin (RNA Pol II), and the lowest H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity (in part) correlates with nucleoli (Nucleolin).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating colocalization of H2B-GFP with H3K9me3.

claim: Lower H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity correlates with euchromatin (RNA Pol II).
source: Fixed epidermal tissue expressing H2B-GFP (green) and co-stained with Hoechst or various subnuclear compartment markers (magenta), demonstrating that high H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity correlates with heterochromatin (H3K9me3), lower H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity correlates with euchromatin (RNA Pol II), and the lowest H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity (in part) correlates with nucleoli (Nucleolin).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating colocalization of H2B-GFP with RNA Pol II.

claim: The lowest H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity (in part) correlates with nucleoli (Nucleolin).
source: Fixed epidermal tissue expressing H2B-GFP (green) and co-stained with Hoechst or various subnuclear compartment markers (magenta), demonstrating that high H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity correlates with heterochromatin (H3K9me3), lower H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity correlates with euchromatin (RNA Pol II), and the lowest H2B-GFP fluorescence intensity (in part) correlates with nucleoli (Nucleolin).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating colocalization of H2B-GFP with Nucleolin.

claim: Applying the histone deacetylase inhibitor Trichostatin-A (TSA) abrogated differences in H2B-GFP fluorescent intensity throughout individual nuclei and resulted in a shifted chromatin compaction curve compared to DMSO vehicle control.
source: Applying the histone deacetylase inhibitor Trichostatin-A (TSA) abrogated these differences in H2B-GFP fluorescent intensity throughout individual nuclei and resulted in a shifted chromatin compaction curve compared to that of epidermal cells in the stem cell layer treated with the DMSO vehicle control (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TSA treatment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and D.

claim: There is clear heterogeneity in chromatin compaction among basal stem cell layer cells.
source: Applying our chromatin compaction analysis to the basal stem cell layer, we noticed a clear heterogeneity among cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the chromatin compaction analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At any given point, ~20% of the cells within the basal layer are in S/G2/M, and the remaining ~80% are in G1.
source: At any given point,~20% of the cells within the basal layer are in S/G2/M, and the remaining ~80% are in G1 (Hiratsuka et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hiratsuka et al., 2015).

claim: Reducing cell cycle heterogeneity by inducing p27 (Cdkn1b) overexpression did not significantly change the population-level chromatin compaction state of basal stem cells.
source: Intriguingly, reducing cell cycle heterogeneity did not significantly change the population-level chromatin compaction state of basal stem cells (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the p27 overexpression experiment shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Wild-type and mutant (p27 overexpressing) populations largely intermix in PHATE analysis both within the homeostatic cell cycle distribution (day 0) and through the cell cycle stall in G1 (day 1).
source: Plotting the combined wild-type and mutant populations together revealed that they largely intermix both within the homeostatic cell cycle distribution (day 0) and through the cell cycle stall in G1 (day 1) (Figure 1G′ and H′), which is in contrast to the largely separated populations of cells treated with TSA vs. DMSO (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D′).
evidence: This claim is supported by PHATE analysis data shown in Figure 1G′ and H′.

claim: Single cell chromatin compaction states in the basal stem cell layer are heterogeneous and independent of interphase cell cycle status.
source: Together, these results show that single cell chromatin compaction states in the basal stem cell layer are heterogeneous and independent of interphase cell cycle status.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the p27 overexpression and PHATE analysis, and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Cells within the stem cell layer will continually alter their transcriptome, delaminate from the stem cell compartment, and move apically/outward to form the overlaying differentiated layer (called spinous) over the course of 3–4 days.
source: Cells within the stem cell layer will continually alter their transcriptome, delaminate from the stem cell compartment, and move apically/outward to form the overlaying differentiated layer (called spinous) over the course of 3–4 days (Cockburn et al., 2022; Mesa et al., 2018; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Cockburn et al., 2022; Mesa et al., 2018) and a schematic figure.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that basal stem cells and differentiated spinous cells have different nuclear volumes and numbers of pericentromeric clusters.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that basal stem cells and differentiated spinous cells have different nuclear volumes and numbers of pericentromeric clusters (Gdula et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Gdula et al., 2013).

claim: Differentiated spinous cells have a higher number of compact, bright chromocenters, and overall flatter nuclei compared to basal stem cells.
source: With live imaging of H2B-GFP, we observe additional qualitative differences in chromatin architecture between these two populations; for example, differentiated spinous cells have a higher number of compact, bright chromocenters, and overall flatter nuclei (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Basal stem cells and differentiated cells have distinct chromatin compaction profiles, where the compaction state of differentiated cells was shifted toward lower fluorescent intensity bins.
source: By applying our chromatin compaction analysis to these two different cell populations, we observed that they have distinct chromatin compaction profiles, where the compaction state of differentiated cells was shifted toward lower fluorescent intensity bins (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The shift left for differentiated cells implies a relative increase in very low-intensity regions such as the nuclear lamina and nucleoli, with a relative decrease in euchromatic and heterochromatin regions.
source: As the quantitative pipeline allows for comparison between nuclei irrespective of differences in mean fluorescent intensity values, the shift left for differentiated cells implies a relative increase in very low-intensity regions such as the nuclear lamina and nucleoli, with a relative decrease in euchromatic and heterochromatin regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the chromatin compaction data based on the normalization method used.

claim: SRF is a transcription factor which helps establish proper cell identity in the epidermis, contributing both to embryonic skin stratification and proper stem cell differentiation in the adult mouse epidermis.
source: SRF is a transcription factor which helps establish proper cell identity in the epidermis, contributing both to embryonic skin stratification and proper stem cell differentiation in the adult mouse epidermis (Lin et al., 2013; Verdoni et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Lin et al., 2013; Verdoni et al., 2010).

claim: At 6 days post-recombination, the loss of SRF caused a transcriptional identity shift in the skin; expression of the basal stem cell marker Keratin-14 was no longer restricted to the basal stem cell layer, despite grossly normal epidermis organization.
source: At 6 days post-recombination, the loss of SRF caused a transcriptional identity shift in the skin; expression of the basal stem cell marker Keratin-14 was no longer restricted to the basal stem cell layer, despite grossly normal epidermis organization (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Expression of Cre did not in itself change chromatin compaction of epidermal cells.
source: Notably, expression of Cre did not in itself change chromatin compaction of epidermal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: By day 6, the differentiated, spinous population's chromatin compaction was more basal-like in the SRF heterozygous mice, while the WT controls maintained distinct chromatin compaction profiles between the cell identities.
source: By day 6, the differentiated, spinous population's chromatin compaction was more basal-like in the SRF heterozygous mice, while the WT controls maintained distinct chromatin compaction profiles between the cell identities (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis data from the SRF experiment shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The chromatin compaction state of spinous differentiated cells shifted towards the chromatin compaction state of basal stem cells in SRF heterozygous mice, reflecting the expansion of Keratin-14 expression into the spinous layer and the breakdown of transcriptome identity between the two cell populations.
source: In particular, the chromatin compaction state of spinous differentiated cells shifted towards the chromatin compaction state of basal stem cells, reflecting the expansion of Keratin-14 expression into the spinous layer and the breakdown of transcriptome identity between the two cell populations.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the SRF experiment data, connecting chromatin compaction changes to transcriptional changes.

claim: Chromatin compaction changes can be reflective of changes in transcriptional program and cell identity, even prior to extensive tissue phenotypes.
source: Importantly, these data also demonstrate that chromatin compaction changes can be reflective of changes in transcriptional program and cell identity, even prior to extensive tissue phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the SRF experiment results.

claim: Chromatin compaction in cells in the basal stem cell layer was relatively stable over 3 hours.
source: Visually, chromatin compaction in cells in the basal stem cell layer was relatively stable over this time. High H2B-GFP density regions appeared to move only slightly, and chromatin compaction profiles at the beginning, middle, and end of these 3-hr time lapses exhibited no significant change at the individual cell or population level (Figure 3A and A′, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A and A′, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Among heterogeneous basal stem cells, the chromatin compaction state of each cell is stable over hours.
source: These findings demonstrated that among these heterogeneous basal stem cells, the chromatin compaction state of each cell is stable over hours.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the 3-hour time-lapse data.

claim: Chromatin of cells actively delaminating (located between the basal and spinous layer) spin over the course of 3 hours.
source: Strikingly, we noticed the chromatin of these cells spin over the course of the timelapse (Figure 3B, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Video 2.

claim: It is likely that the entire nucleus of delaminating cells is rotating, based on observations of nuclear spinning in other systems.
source: The H2B-GFP allele allows us to only visualize spinning of the chromatin, but it is likely that the entire nucleus of these cells is rotating, based on observations of nuclear spinning in other systems (Kumar et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on observations in other systems, supported by citations (Kumar et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2018).

claim: Even as the chromatin as a whole spun in delaminating cells, there were no significant changes in chromatin compaction over 3 hours.
source: Surprisingly, even as the chromatin as a whole spun, there were no significant changes in chromatin compaction (Figure 3B′).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis of spinning cells shown in Figure 3B′.

claim: The chromatin compaction state of actively delaminating cells was markedly different from the chromatin compaction state of basal cells, and appeared to be an intermediate differentiation state between basal and spinous cells.
source: Notably, though, the chromatin compaction state of these actively delaminating cells was markedly different from the chromatin compaction state of basal cells (compare 3B′ to 3 A′), and appeared to be an intermediate differentiation state between basal and spinous cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of chromatin compaction data between different cell populations shown in Figure 3A′ and 3B′.

claim: The transition in chromatin compaction state during epidermal differentiation occurs over days, not hours, and is already in progress during basal cell delamination.
source: Overall, these timelapse data suggest the transition in chromatin compaction state during epidermal differentiation occurs over days, not hours, and is already in progress during basal cell delamination.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the time-lapse data comparing basal and delaminating cells.

claim: A tracked population of basal cells increased their average minimum distance from collagen from day 1 to day 4, reflecting that a portion of these cells were differentiating and moving apically into the spinous layer of the epidermis.
source: This population increased their average minimum distance from collagen from day 1 to day 4, reflecting that a portion of these cells were differentiating and moving apically into the spinous layer of the epidermis (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal tracking data shown in Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A gradual and directional change in chromatin compaction state was observed as cells moved farther from collagen and moved into the spinous layer.
source: When the chromatin compaction analysis was applied to these populations, we observed a gradual and directional change in chromatin compaction state as cells moved farther from collagen and moved into the spinous layer (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis of tracked cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Chromatin compaction remodels slowly over days concomitant with differentiation and delamination.
source: Together, our results indicate that chromatin compaction remodels slowly over days concomitant with differentiation and delamination.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the longitudinal tracking data.

claim: Basal stem cell differentiation involves cumulative transcriptional changes that begin prior to delamination.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that basal stem cell differentiation involves cumulative transcriptional changes that begin prior to delamination (Aragona et al., 2020; Cockburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Aragona et al., 2020; Cockburn et al., 2022).

claim: Expression of Keratin-10 represents a relatively large portion of the basal stem cell layer (~40%).
source: This population represents a relatively large portion of the basal stem cell layer (~40%), and expression of the K10 reporter has been shown to define a point of commitment for delamination (Cockburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Cockburn et al., 2022).

claim: Expression of the K10 reporter has been shown to define a point of commitment for delamination.
source: This population represents a relatively large portion of the basal stem cell layer (~40%), and expression of the K10 reporter has been shown to define a point of commitment for delamination (Cockburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Cockburn et al., 2022).

claim: Basal cells positive for the K10 reporter and K10-negative basal cells had significantly different chromatin compaction profiles.
source: Remarkably, even this relatively small difference in cell states (all a part of the basal stem cell layer) had significantly different chromatin compaction profiles (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The cells positive for the K10 reporter adopted an intermediate chromatin compaction profile which was shifted towards that of the fully differentiated cells.
source: In addition, the cells positive for the K10 reporter adopted an intermediate chromatin compaction profile which was shifted towards that of the fully differentiated cells in Figure 2C and delaminating/differentiating cells in Figure 3B′.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of chromatin compaction profiles across different figures.

claim: Basal stem cells initiate global chromatin changes coinciding with delamination and exit from the stem cell compartment.
source: These data highlight that basal stem cells initiate global chromatin changes coinciding with delamination and exit from the stem cell compartment.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the K10 reporter chromatin compaction data.

claim: PHATE analysis and unsupervised Louvain clustering of basal stem cell chromatin compaction data (including both K10- and K10+ cells) revealed five distinct clusters.
source: Applying the PHATE analysis and an unsupervised Louvain clustering algorithm to this basal stem cell dataset (including both K10- and K10+ cells), five distinct clusters emerged (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PHATE and clustering analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The chromatin compaction profiles of the cells in the five clusters showed an entire spread of curves from most 'basal-like' (cluster 1) to nearly fully differentiated (cluster 5), reflecting the overall differentiation trajectory of chromatin compaction states.
source: The chromatin compaction profiles of the cells in the five clusters showed an entire spread of curves from most 'basal-like' (cluster 1) to nearly fully differentiated (cluster 5) (Figure 4D′), reflecting the overall differentiation trajectory of chromatin compaction states.
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis of the clusters shown in Figure 4D′.

claim: The distribution of K10+ and K10- cells within the PHATE map clusters reinforced the directionality of chromatin compaction changes.
source: The distribution of K10+ and K10- cells within the PHATE map clusters (Figure 4E′) reinforced the directionality of chromatin compaction changes indicated in Figure 4D′.
evidence: This claim is supported by the distribution analysis shown in Figure 4E′.

claim: Changes in chromatin compaction coincides with stem cell commitment to differentiation.
source: Together, these data show that changes in chromatin compaction coincides with stem cell commitment to differentiation.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the K10 reporter and clustering data.

claim: The K10-MS2/MCP-GFP transcription reporter can capture cells at an earlier stage of Keratin-10 expression compared to the K10rtTA reporter.
source: Importantly, while both the K10-MS2/MCP-GFP transcription reporter and the K10rtTA reporter in Figure 4 will capture cells that have been stably expressing Keratin-10 for some time, the transcription reporter can capture cells at an earlier stage of Keratin-10 expression compared to the K10rtTA reporter, which relies on multiple successive steps of gene expression, translation, and recombination.
evidence: This claim is based on the mechanistic differences between the two reporter systems.

claim: Differentiated spinous cells had active transcription of Keratin-10, and only a subset of cells in the basal stem cell layer had active Keratin-10 transcription at any given time.
source: Imaging the epidermis of these mice confirmed that differentiated spinous cells had active transcription of Keratin-10, and only a subset of cells in the basal stem cell layer had active Keratin-10 transcription at any given time (Figure 5B and C), which is consistent with previous characterizations of Keratin-10 protein expression patterns (Braun et al., 2003; Doupé et al., 2010; Schweizer et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B and C and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Keratin-10 transcription primarily occurred within loosely packed euchromatic regions of the nucleus.
source: This analysis revealed that Keratin-10 transcription primarily occurred within loosely packed euchromatic regions of the nucleus (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis of the K10 transcription site shown in Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 15% of basal cells had a strong MCP-GFP punctum in the nucleus at any given time, indicating active transcription.
source: Interestingly, while 15% of basal cells had a strong MCP-GFP punctum in the nucleus at any given time (Figure 5F), indicating active transcription, we also observed cells with multiple, dimmer MCP-GFP puncta in the cytosol without active transcription of Keratin-10 (no nuclear punctum) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Of the cells actively transcribing Keratin-10, about 25% sustained Keratin-10 transcription with no notable change in fluorescence intensity, but about 75% displayed dynamic transcription over the timelapse.
source: Intriguingly, of the cells actively transcribing Keratin-10, about 25% sustained Keratin-10 transcription with no notable change in fluorescence intensity, but about 75% displayed dynamic transcription over the timelapse – they turned Keratin-10 on or turned Keratin-10 off during the hour imaged (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The K10MS2 allele displayed a wide range in both total transcriptional activity and transcriptional burst duration, ranging from a single time step during imaging (3 min) to fully active for the duration of the time lapse (1.25 hr).
source: The K10MS2 allele displayed a wide range in both total transcriptional activity and transcriptional burst duration, ranging from a single time step during imaging (3 min) to fully active for the duration of the time lapse (1.25 hr) (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of transcriptional dynamics shown in Figure 5I–J.

claim: Basal cells actively transcribing Keratin-10 ranged in a burst frequency of 1 (transcribing for the whole hour) to greater than 4.
source: Finally, basal cells actively transcribing Keratin-10 ranged in a burst frequency of 1 (transcribing for the whole hour) to greater than 4 (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of burst frequency shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Fast transcriptional dynamics (transcriptional 'bursting') which have been thoroughly characterized in cell culture and other model organisms are mirrored for this mammalian differentiation gene in vivo.
source: These data indicate that the fast transcriptional dynamics (transcriptional 'bursting') which have been thoroughly characterized in cell culture and other model organisms (Dar et al., 2012; Suter et al., 2011; Bothma et al., 2014; Chubb et al., 2006; Fritzsch et al., 2018) are mirrored for this mammalian differentiation gene in vivo.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the K10 transcriptional dynamics data and is supported by citations to studies on transcriptional bursting.

claim: Only a subset of cells displayed the same transcriptional behaviors between 2 days – approximately 40% of Keratin-10 'on' cells were 'on' the next day, while roughly 60% Keratin-10 'dynamic' cells were 'dynamic' the next day.
source: We observed that only a subset of cells displayed the same transcriptional behaviors between the 2 days – approximately 40% of Keratin-10 'on' cells were 'on' the next day, while roughly 60% Keratin-10 'dynamic' cells were 'dynamic' the next day.
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal tracking of transcriptional dynamics.

claim: The remaining cells which had been transcribing Keratin-10 on day 1 displayed a variety of different Keratin-10 transcriptional behaviors on day 2, including an absence of active transcription entirely.
source: The remaining cells which had been transcribing Keratin-10 on day 1 displayed a variety of different Keratin-10 transcriptional behaviors on day 2, including an absence of active transcription entirely (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal tracking data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Keratin-10 transcriptional activity in basal stem cells is flexibly dynamic across days as well as minutes.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that Keratin-10 transcriptional activity in basal stem cells is flexibly dynamic across days as well as minutes.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the longitudinal transcriptional dynamics data.

claim: Cells actively transcribing Keratin-10 had chromatin compaction states similar to that of cells not transcribing Keratin-10.
source: This analysis revealed that cells actively transcribing Keratin-10 had chromatin compaction states similar to that of cells not transcribing Keratin-10 (Figure 5H and H′, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), although they trended towards the chromatin compaction state of cells expressing the K10rtTA reporter (compare Figure 5H to Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis shown in Figure 5H and H′, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Chromatin compaction changes either have not yet occurred or are just beginning to occur when Keratin-10 transcription is initiated.
source: Because the cells marked by the Keratin-10-MS2/MCP-GFP transcription reporter include those at the very earliest step of differentiation, this result suggests that chromatin compaction changes either have not yet occurred or are just beginning to occur when Keratin-10 transcription is initiated.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the chromatin compaction data from K10-transcribing cells.

claim: The chromatin compaction signature of Keratin-10 'on' compared to Keratin-10 'dynamic' cells were extremely close to one another, suggesting that the cells displaying these different Keratin-10 transcriptional dynamics in fact co-exist within extremely similar cell identity states.
source: Intriguingly, the chromatin compaction signature of Keratin-10 'on' compared to Keratin-10 'dynamic' cells were extremely close to one another (Figure 5M) suggesting that the cells displaying these different Keratin-10 transcriptional dynamics in fact co-exist within extremely similar cell identity states.
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin compaction analysis shown in Figure 5M and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: The initiation of Keratin-10 transcription, which represents one of the first steps of a basal stem cell towards differentiation, is highly dynamic and significant chromatin remodeling occurs after transcription initiation of Keratin-10.
source: Altogether, these results reveal that the initiation of Keratin-10 transcription, which represents one of the first steps of a basal stem cell towards differentiation, is highly dynamic and that significant chromatin remodeling occurs after transcription initiation of Keratin-10.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the K10 transcription and chromatin compaction data.

claim: Stem cells undergo a relatively large reorganization of their genome through the differentiation process as their cell identity changes.
source: Stem cells undergo a relatively large reorganization of their genome through the differentiation process as their cell identity changes (Kurimoto et al., 2015; Oudelaar et al., 2020; Paulsen et al., 2019; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Current tools offer high-resolution data about the chromatin environment at specific loci, but rely on fixed cells and are unable to reveal how chromatin architecture is remodeled during cell identity changes such as differentiation.
source: Current tools offer high-resolution data about the chromatin environment at specific loci, but rely on fixed cells and are unable to reveal how chromatin architecture is remodeled during cell identity changes such as differentiation.
evidence: This claim represents a statement about the limitations of current methodologies in the field.

claim: Through high-resolution imaging of H2B-GFP in live mice, chromatin compaction heterogeneity was discovered within the epidermal stem cell population under homeostatic equilibrium.
source: Here, through high-resolution imaging of H2B-GFP in live mice, we discovered chromatin compaction heterogeneity within the epidermal stem cell population under homeostatic equilibrium.
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding from the study.

claim: This heterogeneity arises from gradual, incremental shifts in stem cell identity throughout differentiation which begin prior to exit from the stem cell layer.
source: This heterogeneity arises from gradual, incremental shifts in stem cell identity throughout differentiation which begin prior to exit from the stem cell layer.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the chromatin compaction and differentiation marker data.

claim: By live imaging endogenous transcription of Keratin-10, highly dynamic transcriptional activity was resolved over hours and days in the absence of significant chromatin architecture changes.
source: Moreover, by live imaging endogenous transcription of Keratin-10, a hallmark of epidermal differentiation, we resolved highly dynamic transcriptional activity over hours and days in the absence of significant chromatin architecture changes.
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding from the K10 transcription imaging experiments.

claim: Most of the global genome reorganization associated with cell identity transitions occurs between the initiation of differentiation-associated transcription and exit from the stem cell layer (delamination).
source: Ultimately, we determined that most of the global genome reorganization associated with cell identity transitions occurs between the initiation of differentiation-associated transcription and exit from the stem cell layer (delamination; Figure 6, model).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined transcription and chromatin compaction data, presented as a model in Figure 6.

claim: Recent studies which performed live imaging in cell culture systems to evaluate chromatin dynamics at finer scales have revealed that chromatin can be locally dynamic over minutes and seconds.
source: Recently, other studies which performed live imaging in cell culture systems to evaluate chromatin dynamics at finer scales, such as individual loci and Topologically Associated Domain (TAD) boundaries, have revealed that chromatin can be locally dynamic over minutes and seconds (Barth et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2018; Gabriele et al., 2022; Iida et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Dynamic local changes to individual loci and TADs may act cumulatively toward a global and incremental shift in chromatin architecture through differentiation.
source: These dynamic local changes to individual loci and TADs may act cumulatively toward a global and incremental shift in chromatin architecture through differentiation.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about how local chromatin dynamics relate to global changes.

claim: Recent work tracking epidermal cell fates over a week showed that differentiating basal cells expressing Keratin-10 are still capable of proliferation.
source: Recent work tracking epidermal cell fates over a week showed that differentiating basal cells expressing Keratin-10 are still capable of proliferation (Cockburn et al., 2022), a behavior that was previously assumed to be unique to epidermal stem cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Cockburn et al., 2022).

claim: Pseudo-time analysis of scRNA-sequencing data revealed a significant population of cells that contain both stem and differentiation-associated transcripts (Keratin-14 and Keratin-10, respectively).
source: Additionally, pseudo-time analysis of scRNA-sequencing data from the same study revealed a significant population of cells that contain both stem and differentiation-associated transcripts (Keratin-14 and Keratin-10, respectively).
evidence: This claim refers to findings from a cited study.

claim: The dynamic nature of Keratin-10 transcription observed within a one-hour timelapse could reflect the fact that many genes exhibit transcriptional bursting kinetics on the scale of minutes.
source: While the dynamic nature of Keratin-10 transcription we observed within a one-hour timelapse could reflect the fact that that many genes exhibit transcriptional bursting kinetics on the scale of minutes (Dar et al., 2012; Suter et al., 2011), the observation that a portion of cells actively transcribing Keratin-10 no longer express it 1 day later supports the idea that individual cells remain somewhat flexible in their initial commitment to differentiation (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the transcriptional dynamics data, supported by citations.

claim: The observation that a portion of cells actively transcribing Keratin-10 no longer express it 1 day later supports the idea that individual cells remain somewhat flexible in their initial commitment to differentiation.
source: While the dynamic nature of Keratin-10 transcription we observed within a one-hour timelapse could reflect the fact that that many genes exhibit transcriptional bursting kinetics on the scale of minutes (Dar et al., 2012; Suter et al., 2011), the observation that a portion of cells actively transcribing Keratin-10 no longer express it 1 day later supports the idea that individual cells remain somewhat flexible in their initial commitment to differentiation (Figure 5L).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the longitudinal transcriptional dynamics data.

claim: Recent papers have supported the bi-directional and reciprocal nature of chromatin organization at individual gene loci and transcription of those loci.
source: Recent papers have supported the bi-directional and reciprocal nature of chromatin organization at individual gene loci and transcription of those loci (Lai et al., 2018; Oudelaar et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Through live imaging approach, understanding of the interplay between the highly dynamic nature of transcription and local chromatin architecture has been greatly enriched by tracking cell identity transitions in a live mammal.
source: Through our live imaging approach, we have greatly enriched our understanding of the interplay between the highly dynamic nature of transcription and local chromatin architecture by tracking cell identity transitions in a live mammal.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement about the contribution of the study.

claim: This chromatin compaction system is not dependent on biology inherent to the skin or epidermis, and is widely applicable to other systems due to the use of H2B-GFP in many model systems.
source: Finally, this chromatin compaction system is not dependent on biology inherent to the skin or epidermis, and in fact is widely applicable to other systems due to the use of H2B-GFP in many model systems.
evidence: This claim is a statement about the potential applicability of the method.

claim: This approach could be used to investigate other biological transitions in cell identity such as oncogenic initiation and expansion, and mesenchymal transitions through wound healing.
